title: Using RL Agent to Detect and Remediate ETL Pipeline Failures - Anna Marie Benzon

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on agent architecture: a layered design separating deterministic rules, Q-learning policy, and external safety constraints, with a bounded six-action space and escalation as a first-class action. ETL pipeline failure remediation is an enterprise operational workflow, and the system automates data infrastructure maintenance tasks across AWS services. The system is evaluated on 30 controlled synthetic runs with production validation explicitly stated as not yet completed. Requires understanding of Q-learning, AWS architecture, agent design patterns, and evaluation methodology with ablation studies and confidence intervals. Single-speaker conference presentation on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. All evidence anchors are directly stated in the transcript with quantitative claims from controlled benchmark runs.

summary: The talk addresses ETL pipeline failures that require engineers to manually inspect logs, diagnose schema or data-quality issues, select a repair, rerun the job, and validate recovery—a process modeled at roughly 2.5 working days per incident. Anna Marie Benzon presents an RL-guided pipeline health agent that automates this workflow through a deliberately layered architecture. The end-to-end AWS architecture begins with an existing AWS Glue ETL job emitting a failure event caught by Amazon EventBridge, which triggers a Lambda function running the agent. Lambda gathers evidence from two read-only sources—CloudWatch for error logs and the Glue Data Catalog for current schema metadata—and uses these to classify the failure, assess data quality and operational risk, and construct a state for the RL decision engine. The intelligence layer separates three concerns: deterministic anomaly rules establish observable facts (field disappearance, type changes, null-rate thresholds); a Q-learning policy handles context-action selection given the current incident state; and a safety override layer sits outside the learn policy, converting passive actions to escalations for critical conditions. Before action selection, deterministic components—schema profiler, drift detector, data quality analyzer, error classifier, and risk scorer—establish what actually happened. These are deterministic by design because explicit rules are easier to validate, explain, and debug than inference. The policy receives a compact state (failure category, risk level, confidence, data quality condition) and selects from six actions: retry, schema coercion, rollback, quarantine, escalate, or log. Q-learning was chosen because state and action spaces are small, making Q-tables cheap and inspectable. Each incident is modeled as a single-step contextual decision rather than a long-horizon control task. The safety layer checks every proposal against operational constraints. Passive actions are overridden for critical conditions, and high-risk or unknown cases are escalated. Escalation is treated as a first-class action, not the agent giving up—correctly recognizing the boundary of its evidence or authority. Every proposal, override, execution result, and validation outcome is written to an audit record in S3. Evaluation across 30 controlled synthetic runs showed mean resolution time of approximately 5.24 minutes for successfully resolved cases, a simulated success rate of 74.63%, and a non-escalation rate of 88.63%. Ablation revealed the RL policy matched the equivalent deterministic policy (0% difference), while random selection performed 15.63 points worse. The safety override reduced non-escalation by about 15 points—intentional, as the guardrail escalates more often when autonomy would be inappropriate. Reliability comes primarily from structured state, sensible decision logic, and external safety constraints, not from RL alone.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Separate deterministic rules for facts, Q-learning for contextual action selection, and external safety constraints—this three-layer separation is the core design principle.

The RL policy matched the equivalent deterministic policy (0% difference), showing RL provides an inspectable learn decision service rather than an immediate success rate advantage in the current benchmark.
Escalation is a first-class action, not the agent giving up—it correctly recognizes the boundary of its evidence or authority.
Mean resolution time of ~5.24 minutes vs. 2.5 working days manual baseline equals ~99.85% MTTR reduction for successfully resolved cases.
Safety overrides reduced non-escalation by ~15 points—intentional, as the guardrail escalates more often when autonomy would be inappropriate.
Reliability comes primarily from structured state, sensible decision logic, and external safety constraints, not from RL alone.
Single-step contextual Q-learning with small state/action spaces enables cheap, inspectable Q-tables rather than requiring complex models.
A single favorable run is a demo, not evidence—evaluate across repeated seeds and compare against simple baselines.
The agent responds after failure signals; it does not predict failures before they happen.
Code, synthetic benchmark experiment scripts, and reproduction instructions are publicly available in the GitHub repository.

sections.title: Problem Motivation and Engineering Objective
sections.summary: ETL failures require manual inspection, diagnosis, repair selection, rerun, and validation—a workflow modeled at ~2.5 working days. Failures include daytime format incompatibility, null-rate spikes, type changes, and runtime errors. The engineering objective is to compress recovery for routine recognizable failures while escalating uncertain, novel, or high-risk cases.

sections.title: End-to-End AWS Architecture
sections.summary: Architecture starts with an existing AWS Glue ETL job emitting a failure event caught by EventBridge, triggering a Lambda function. Lambda gathers evidence from CloudWatch (error logs) and Glue Data Catalog (schema metadata), classifies the failure, assesses data quality and operational risk, and constructs state for the RL decision engine. The safety layer checks proposals before the executor uses Glue API to retrigger or apply remediation. S3 stores audit artifacts and quarantine outputs.

sections.title: Intelligence Layer Design and Deterministic Components
sections.summary: Three concerns are deliberately separated: deterministic anomaly rules for observable facts, Q-learning policy for context-action selection, and safety override outside the learn policy. Deterministic components—schema profiler, drift detector, data quality analyzer, error classifier, and risk scorer—establish what actually happened before action selection. ML-ready is not the same as ML-required; the simplest reliable component should win each decision.

sections.title: Q-Learning Policy and Safety Layer
sections.summary: Policy receives compact state (failure category, risk level, confidence, data quality condition) and selects from six actions: retry, coercion, rollback, quarantine, escalate, or log. Q-learning chosen because state/action spaces are small, making Q-tables cheap and inspectable. Each incident is a single-step contextual decision, not long-horizon control. The learn policy proposes; the safety layer checks against operational constraints and overrides passive actions for critical conditions. Escalation is a first-class action, not giving up.

sections.title: Failure Path Example
sections.summary: Example: agent receives Glue-style job failure, log classifier detects datetime format incompatibility at 0.9 confidence, policy proposes schema coercion, safety override does not fire (not critical), but executor discovers automatic coercion unavailable for this case. System reports execution unavailable and sends incident for manual review—showing two distinct controls: policy safety and implementation capability.

sections.title: Benchmark Setup and Evaluation Results
sections.summary: Public benchmark built around generalized AWS Lambda-style architecture with client-provided synthetic data for capstone and newly generated synthetic schemas/logs/scenarios for public repo. No client documents or identifiers. Rule-based detector: precision 1.0, recall 0.8, F1 0.889. Successful resolution time ~5.24 minutes across 30 runs. Success rate 74.63% ± 1.51%. Non-escalation rate 88.63% ± 0.89%. MTTR reduction ~99.85% vs. 2.5-day baseline.

sections.title: Ablation Results and Validation Boundary
sections.summary: RL policy matched equivalent deterministic policy (0% difference within 0.19 point CI). Random selection was 15.63 points worse. Safety override reduced non-escalation ~15 points (intentional). Reliability comes from structured state, sensible logic, and external constraints, not RL alone. Validation boundary: synthetic scenarios only, responds after failure not before, some actions simulated/bounded, production validation is next step.

sections.title: Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Five takeaways: use deterministic logic for measurable facts, learning only for contextual action selection, safety constraints outside the learn policy, treat escalation and validation as first-class outcomes, and evaluate across repeated seeds against simple baselines. Goal is not to eliminate human judgment but to stop spending it on recognizable 2am failures. High-risk failures still go to humans. Code and benchmark available on GitHub.
